wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e111.summary: Poses the second preliminary question for the fourth principal question: whether practical and speculative knowledge are distinguished by their ends or by their objects. For ends: Metaphysics II says the end of speculative knowledge is truth and of practical knowledge, work. Against this: Avicenna says practical sciences concern our works and speculative ones do not, which points to objects.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e135.summary: Reports an opinion that speculative and practical science are distinguished by their ends. It distinguishes the end of the science (what the science is ordered to) from the end of the knower (what the knower orders it to), and the per se, principal end from the per accidens, secondary end. A science is called speculative or practical not by the knower's end but by its own per se principal end: ordered by nature to knowing truth (speculative) or to doing good (practical).
claims: A science is speculative or practical by its per se principal end, not the knower's end (reported).
The end of the science differs from the end of the knower (reported).
concepts: per se vs. per accidens end

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e174.summary: First argument for the opinion: each effect is distinguished by its nobler cause, and the final cause is the noblest, the 'cause of causes' (Avicenna). So practical knowledge is distinguished from speculative by its end: work versus truth.
claims: Effects are distinguished by their noblest cause (reported).
The final cause is the cause of causes (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e194.summary: Second argument: a science is distinguished by subject or by end. Practical and speculative knowledge are not distinguished by subject, since both can concern the same subject, so they are distinguished by end.
claims: Speculative and practical science can share a subject (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e208.summary: Third argument: as principles are in speculative matters, so is the end in practical ones (Physics II). Speculative sciences are distinguished by their principles, so practical ones by ends, as Metaphysics II and De anima III say. Ockham then begins his critique, arguing that practical and speculative knowledge are not distinguished by distinct final causes, since the same thing can be the final cause of both. The end of the science is the same as the end of the knower, and one and the same end can move a knower to acquire both kinds of science. The end of any action is what the agent intends, or what a superior directing agent intends, as in nature the end of lower agents and of the directing intelligence is the same.
claims: The end of the science and the end of the knower are the same.
The same end can be the final cause of both speculative and practical science.
The end of an action is the end intended by the agent or by a directing superior agent.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e254.summary: Further: an end relates to form or matter only through the agent, insofar as it moves the efficient cause to act, that is, insofar as it is intended. So something is a final cause only by being intended, and the end intended by the agent and the end of the form are the same.
claims: An end causes only by moving the agent to act.
Something is a final cause only insofar as it is intended.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e274.summary: Further: nothing is an essential cause of a thing on which the thing depends neither in being nor in becoming. A thing does not depend in any way on what does not move the efficient cause to act, neither in being (it exists without it) nor in becoming (it comes to be anyway).
claims: An essential cause is something on which the effect depends in being or becoming.
What does not move the agent is no cause of the effect.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e287.summary: Further: what a thing essentially depends on, so that without it the thing would have no real being, is its essential cause. A science really depends on the knower's end: if someone would learn a speculative science only for profit, then without that intention the science would not exist. So the knower's end is a cause, and only a final cause.
claims: A science depends really on the end for which the knower acquires it.
The knower's end is a final cause of the science.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e309.summary: Further: what answers the question 'why?' has the character of a final cause, and the knower's end answers 'why does this science exist?'
claims: Whatever answers 'why?' has the character of a final cause.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e320.summary: Ockham's own answer begins by distinguishing two senses of 'end'. (1) Something to be acquired by an operation, as health is the end of walking, loved with love of concupiscence. (2) The end loved with love of friendship, for whose sake the first is produced: a person loves themself and desires health for themself, or loves God supremely and acts for God, so God is the end of all acts. The first is first in intention and last in execution, an effect, and usually less noble than the agent. The second usually pre-exists the operation, is not less noble than what is for its sake, and is not, properly speaking, an effect acquired by the operation. (The transcription is partly corrupt.)
claims: 'End' means either an object acquired by operation (loved with concupiscence) or a beloved for whose sake one acts (loved with friendship).
God can be the end of all acts as loved for his own sake.
The end-to-be-acquired is first in intention and last in execution.
concepts: first in intention, last in execution

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e358.summary: Second thesis: properly, the end of a science is what the learner loves, with love of friendship or concupiscence, and what moves them to learn. So the final cause of the knower and of the science is the same, not in that it causes the knower, but in that what the agent intends and loves is the final cause of the science. Example: someone who learns out of friendship-love for themself, desiring the science for profit, is themself the final cause of the science. The science follows on their being loved, though they do not cause or depend on themself.
claims: The end of a science is what the learner loves and what moves them to learn.
A learner loving themself can be the final cause of the science.
Something can be a cause in the sense that upon its being another follows.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e410.summary: Likewise, profit or the like is in a way a final cause of the science, since it answers 'why learn it?' It is not a final cause of the knower, who does not depend on it essentially, but only what the knower desires and for which they act to acquire the science.
claims: The intended benefit is a final cause of the science, not of the knower.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e432.summary: Supports this by analogy: as in natural agents the final cause is what nature intends, so in voluntary agents it is what the will intends. Profit is intended by the will and the science is produced for it, so it is a final cause of the science, not of the knower.
claims: In voluntary agency the final cause is what the will intends.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e448.summary: Further: what the divine will intends in causing is a final cause, not of God but of the effect, and by parity the same holds for what a created will intends.
claims: What the divine will intends is a final cause of the effect, not of God.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e457.summary: On this account God is the final cause of all things, being always loved and all things being made for his sake, at least by himself. In nature the end of the natural agent and of the supreme directing agent is the same. To fit common usage, Ockham distinguishes two ends of a science: (1) the proper final cause for which it is acquired and which moves the agent; (2) the end that a free agent ought to intend according to right reason. In the second sense the end of practical science is work or operating and of speculative science is considering. If a learner does not in fact intend these, they are not final causes, since the sciences do not depend on them; the actually intended ends are.
claims: God is the final cause of all things.
The end of a science can be the actually intended end or the end that right reason prescribes.
By right reason, the end of practical science is operation and of speculative science is consideration.
An end not actually intended is not a final cause.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e496.summary: Answers the objection that a final cause need only be apt to be intended, not actually intended. A final cause must actually cause if the effect exists, and it causes only if actually intended. Two further objections are noted: this contradicts Aristotle (De anima III, Metaphysics VI and II), and a thing has one essential final cause, while on this view it would have many, since many ends can be intended.
claims: A final cause must be actually intended to cause.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e521.summary: Answers the appeal to authorities: they concern the end that should be intended according to right reason, at least usually, if all were properly ordered, so that the science is as if by nature ordinable to it. If not actually intended, it is not truly and properly a final cause.
claims: Aristotle's statements concern the end prescribed by right reason, not the actual final cause.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e534.summary: Answers the plurality objection: just as one thing can have several proper efficient causes, each sufficient among secondary causes (heat from fire without the sun or from the sun without fire), so it can have several final causes, each sufficient in its order. One final cause can likewise cause many specifically distinct sciences and effects. Third thesis: things are distinguished by intrinsic factors (man and ass by their substantial forms) or by extrinsic ones, whether by causes of their distinction (limited or unlimited) or by what is proper to them (properties, subjects, effects). So these sciences are distinguished intrinsically and formally by themselves, since they are simple forms. They are distinguished causally by ends, as by efficient causes, since a thing has its being and its distinct being from the same cause, even if both share one final cause, as God distinguishes all creatures. They are not necessarily distinguished by subjects in any of these ways, but are distinguished by objects, the known conclusions, as by something proper to them. 'Nothing is distinguished by what it shares' holds of proper distinguishers, not of an unlimited cause.
claims: A thing can have several sufficient efficient or final causes.
Sciences, being simple forms, are distinguished intrinsically only by themselves.
Sciences are distinguished causally by their ends, even when they share one end.
God, as cause of all, is the cause of the distinction of all creatures.
Sciences are not necessarily distinguished by subjects.
Speculative and practical sciences are distinguished by their objects, the known conclusions.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e651.summary: Adds that taking 'end' as what right reason prescribes, the sciences are distinguished by ends as by something proper, since each has a different end. This is how Aristotle means it in De anima III and Metaphysics II, though these ends are not always final causes properly speaking.
claims: Taking ends as prescribed by right reason, practical and speculative sciences have proper and distinct ends.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e669.summary: Proves that the sciences are not distinguished by subjects. Not formally, since the subject is neither the science nor part of its essence. Not causally, since in this life the subject is often a being of reason (on one opinion) and causes nothing, or God alone could cause the science. Not as by something proper, since one subject can be the subject of both: earth has properties not in our power (round, cold, dry, heavy), known by natural science, and others in our power (arable, cultivable), known by agriculture. Every natural being that is matter for artificial forms is likewise, as are man and the intellective soul. Practical conclusions can be deduced, at least mediately or particularly, from speculative principles: from 'earth is hard' follows the need to plough it, and from man's condition, medical prescriptions. Such principles may be called virtually practical, but in common usage are speculative, or else no principle would be purely speculative; even 'every triangle has three angles...' yields practical knowledge in the mechanical arts. That practical sciences are subalternated to speculative ones (music to arithmetic) also shows that practical conclusions resolve into speculative principles. Fourth thesis: the sciences are distinguished by their known conclusions as something proper. A speculative conclusion contains nothing doable by us, while a practical one contains or imports something doable. So practical knowledge must have praxis, or what signifies praxis, as at least its partial object, and must direct more than incomplex knowledge of its terms. It follows that there can be speculative science of our works (that love is a quality dependent on God), which is why De anima can be speculative, and that logic, rhetoric and grammar are truly practical, since they direct the intellect's will-governed operations.
claims: Sciences are not distinguished formally, causally or properly by their subjects.
The same subject (earth, man, soul) can be the subject of speculative and practical knowledge.
Practical conclusions can be derived from speculative principles.
Subalternation of practical to speculative sciences shows that practical conclusions resolve into speculative principles.
Practical and speculative sciences are distinguished by the conclusions known.
Practical knowledge has praxis or something signifying praxis as at least a partial object.
Practical knowledge must direct more than incomplex knowledge of its terms.
There can be speculative science of our own works.
Logic, rhetoric and grammar are practical sciences.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e893.summary: Distinguishes two kinds of practical knowledge. Dictative knowledge determinately dictates that something is to be done or not, as in Ethics VI and De anima III; in this sense logic, rhetoric and the mechanical arts are not practical, since none dictates that a house is to be built, which belongs to prudence. Ostensive knowledge dictates nothing to pursue or avoid but only shows how a work can be done, so that if the intellect dictates it and the will wills it, one can at once act rightly: building shows that a house is made of wood and stone with a certain foundation, walls and roof. Logic and other arts are ostensive and directive, not dictative, and such arts often have the object of praxis, not praxis itself, as their object (the house, not the building).
claims: Practical knowledge is either dictative or ostensive.
Dictative practical knowledge belongs to prudence.
Logic, rhetoric and mechanical arts are ostensive, not dictative.
Arts often have the object of praxis, not praxis itself, as object.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e954.summary: Raises a doubt: it would follow that every practical habit apart from these arts is prudence, so that the Ethics would be prudence. That is false, since the Ethics concerns universals and prudence particulars. The consequence holds because every dictative habit is active with reason, and so is prudence.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e973.summary: Reports Scotus's reply: the definition of prudence should be understood of a proximate active habit, acquired from acts. As art relates to experiential habit for singular makeables, moral science relates to prudence for doables. Art and moral science are universal and remote in directing, while prudence and experience, generated from acts, are particular and proximate. Scotus deems this necessary, since otherwise no science would be practical.
claims: Moral science and art are remote universal directive habits; prudence and experience are proximate (Scotus, reported).

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e997.summary: Ockham rejects the claim that a universal habit is not proximately directive. As in speculative matters, whoever has a universal proposition and subsumes a singular knows the conclusion at once. So whoever has the universal 'one should act thus at such time and place' needs only to be shown something with those conditions to act at once. If such showing is required, the habit of prudence also needs it, so the universal habit directs as well as any habit regarding some acts. Also, such universals are known evidently only by experience, so experience is presupposed and the habit directs immediately.
claims: A universal practical proposition plus a subsumed singular suffices for action.
Prudence also requires presentation of the particular case.
Universal practical principles are known only through experience.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e1036.summary: Concludes that a universal habit can, for its part, direct some act as perfectly as any other habit, can often be had without experience of singulars, and would still direct perfectly. This seems to contradict Metaphysics I, where art can exist without experience and the experienced act more surely.
claims: A universal habit can direct an act as perfectly as any other habit.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e1054.summary: Interprets Aristotle: the experienced act more surely in two ways. (1) Through bodily exercise of organs: a practiced cithara player performs better than someone with a better intellectual habit gained by listening, as in medicine and arts needing exterior work. (2) Because the experienced know some singular and universal propositions that others lack evidently, learned by experience without knowing the cause, while the artisan knows the cause in general, as in subalternating science. Such less universal propositions direct more immediately. Artisans have evident knowledge because in practical matters, as in others, some principles are self-evident and some known only by experience. Artisans and untrained moral philosophers know the former and what follows, which experts often lack. Of the latter, sometimes artisans and sometimes experts have evident knowledge. So an artisan can know more while an expert acts more surely, and the least universal knowledge directs as perfectly as any habit. A moral philosopher who acquired all the universal propositions of a practiced person, without moral acts, would have as perfect a directive habit, but in fact this is impossible or very hard. That is why, as Book III will show, prudence cannot be separated from moral virtue in its acquisition.
claims: The experienced act more surely through trained bodily organs or through experiential knowledge of less universal propositions.
In practical matters some principles are self-evident and some known only by experience.
An artisan can know more while an expert acts more surely.
Someone with all the relevant universal propositions would have an equally perfect directive habit without practice.
In fact prudence cannot be acquired apart from moral virtue.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e1169.summary: Distinguishes moral science from prudence as more and less universal habits: moral science concerns more universal propositions, while prudence concerns less universal ones known only by experience, not deduced. Prudence concerns particulars in acquisition, factually and virtually, to be discussed in Book III. Then the formal answer: speculative and practical sciences are distinguished by ends causally, since the end causes both the sciences and their distinction. Taking 'end' as what right reason prescribes, they are distinguished by ends as by proper features. They are distinguished by subjects in neither way, but by objects in the second way. Replies: the first opposing argument is answered by causal distinction through the end (same or different) and proper distinction through the right-reason end.
claims: Moral science and prudence differ as more and less universal habits.
Prudence concerns less universal propositions known only by experience.
Speculative and practical sciences are distinguished causally by ends and properly by their right-reason ends and objects.
They are not distinguished by subjects.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e1224.summary: Further replies. To the second argument: speculative and practical sciences are distinguished by objects, the known conclusions. To the third: speculative sciences are distinguished by themselves but by their principles as by proper features, and principles in speculative sciences are not like the end in practical ones, especially if 'end' means the proper final cause. Aristotle's 'distinguished by end' means only that practical science has a different right-reason end. Generally, nothing is properly distinguished except by itself or something intrinsic, just as each thing is one by itself. Something is said to be distinguished 'by' a feature when that feature is proper to one and cannot belong to the other, so that distinctness of the features entails distinctness of their bearers. Corporeal and spiritual qualities entail distinct subjects, whereas whiteness and sweetness do not (milk has both). So spiritual substance is 'distinguished' from corporeal by its quality, while milk is not distinguished from a swan by whiteness.
claims: Practical and speculative sciences are distinguished by their known conclusions.
Nothing is properly distinguished except by itself or something intrinsic.
To be 'distinguished by' a feature means that the feature is proper and entails distinction of bearers.

wo8uy7-d1e191-d1e1286.summary: Answers the principal argument: the right-reason end of practical science is a work apt to be directed by it, though that work is not always a proper final cause. In Aristotle's sense, the end of practical science is not truth, as it is for speculative science. The ultimate end of speculative science is truth and that of practical science is work.
claims: The right-reason end of practical science is work, not truth.
The ultimate end of speculative science is truth.

wo8uy7-d1e191.summary: Prologue question 11, the second preliminary to the question whether theology is practical, asks whether practical and speculative knowledge are distinguished by ends or by objects. Ockham rejects the view that they are distinguished by the science's own per se end as opposed to the knower's end. The end of the science and of the knower are the same, and an end is a final cause only by actually moving the agent through being loved and intended, whether as a beloved for whose sake one acts (love of friendship) or as a good to be acquired (concupiscence). God is thus the final cause of all things. Sciences, being simple forms, are distinguished intrinsically by themselves. They are distinguished causally by their ends, even a shared one, and properly by the ends right reason prescribes (operation versus consideration). They are not distinguished by subjects, since earth, man or the soul can be subjects of both kinds and practical conclusions derive from speculative principles, but they are distinguished by their objects, the known conclusions. Practical knowledge has praxis or something signifying it as at least a partial object and directs more than incomplex knowledge does. So there can be speculative knowledge of our works, and logic, rhetoric and grammar are practical. He distinguishes dictative practical knowledge (prudence) from ostensive knowledge (arts, logic). Against Scotus, he argues that universal practical knowledge can be proximately directive. He explains why experienced practitioners act more surely, distinguishes moral science from prudence by degree of universality, and offers a general account of what it means to be 'distinguished by' something.
claims: Practical and speculative sciences are distinguished by their objects (known conclusions), not their subjects.
Sciences are distinguished causally by ends, and properly by ends prescribed by right reason.
A final cause is a final cause only by being actually intended.
Logic, rhetoric and grammar are practical sciences.
Practical knowledge is either dictative (prudence) or ostensive (arts).
Universal practical knowledge can be as directive as prudence.
Moral science and prudence differ by degree of universality.
